extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and readers interested in research integrity and scholarly publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the integrity and quality of journal peer review and editorial processes, especially regarding special issues and signs of paper-mill or manipulated reviews. Includes recognizing red flags, enforcement practices, and retraction management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compromised peer review / manipulated identities and fabricated content
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers identified with compromised peer review where researcher identities were manipulated (to appear as legitimate researchers) and content fabricated (to appear as legitimate content).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These compromised papers were concentrated in special issues and targeted by papermills and bad actors; such evidence is a basis for mass retractions (publisher statement: "The Special Issues in these journals were targeted by papermills and bad actors, with researcher identities manipulated... and content fabricated...").

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of paper mill activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Identification of indicators that a set of articles may be produced by paper mills, prompting publisher investigation and potential retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers have issued mass retractions after identifying such signs (examples: IOP Publishing retracted nearly 500 articles; PLOS retracted over 100). The article implies publishers should proactively look for patterns across journals and special issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special-issue oversight and quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Special issues require adequate editorial oversight; lack of oversight can allow large numbers of low-quality or fraudulent papers to be published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters note publishers often 'farm out' special issues with insufficient oversight, letting guest editors or systems fill issues with nonsense. The chief editor of a special issue is responsible for the papers they publish; publishers should not abdicate standards for special issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor responsibility to evaluate content (not just count reviewer votes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must examine manuscript content themselves and not merely count reviewer recommendations when deciding to accept or reject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism in comments: 'The editor simply goes for the vote of the majority.' An editor's role 'ALSO is to look [at] the content, not merely count votes.' Failure to do so is a red flag for compromised review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerabilities of blinded review; call for transparency/open review
rubrics_metrics.description: Blind (anonymous) peer review can be exploited or fail to detect manipulation; some argue for transparent/open review where reviewer identities are disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment: 'I think the fake publications make use of what is called blind review policy... The review process must be transparent, open and available to public for commenting. Donot give any research item for review or comment to who donot want disclose his identity.' This identifies blind review as a vulnerability and transparency as a proposed mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag: unusually large number of authors requiring provenance of contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers with too many authors should be flagged and require convincing justification that all listed authors made real contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from Hindawi practice: they flag articles with too many authors and may reject without review unless authors can demonstrate real roles for all contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of author contact information and institutional affiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Author email addresses and institutional affiliations should be verifiable; lack of verifiable contact details is a red flag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hindawi reportedly checks that author emails are identifiable (e.g., previous publication or academic email) and may require letters from department heads or university officials confirming an author's status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforceable peer-review standards and their active enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals must have clear peer-review standards for submissions and enforce them consistently; standards alone are insufficient without enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments note that many publishers have standards for peer review and special issues but that standards are sometimes neglected by reviewers or guest editors. Effective enforcement (not just policy) is required to maintain quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers should not accept papers merely for revenue or as 'paid-for' content
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepting manuscripts for payment or as a revenue strategy without rigorous review damages journal credibility and may constitute predatory behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentary: 'Publishers cannot have it both ways. Either you are a serious publisher and impose standards on what you publish, or you are a predatory publisher and print anything that’s paid for.' Financial motives should not override quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction process design: fairness and scalability for mass retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction procedures should be designed to handle mass retractions efficiently while treating affected parties fairly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiley stated it is 'designing a new retraction process that will help us, and potentially others, accelerate and deal with this new era of mass retractions fairly.' Publishers should develop transparent, consistent processes for large-scale corrective actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing and external quality criteria (e.g., Clarivate Web of Science standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals are subject to external indexing and quality assessments; failure to meet those criteria can lead to delisting, reflecting deficiencies in quality control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example in article: Clarivate dropped 19 Hindawi journals from Web of Science for failing to meet quality criteria; indexing actions can be a consequence and signal of systemic problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms for reporting problematic articles and providing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be clear channels for readers to report suspected problematic or unscientific articles, accompanied by instructions to provide accurate evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters provided specific email addresses to report concerns and advised reporters to document evidence and indicate if papers belong to special issues; journals/publishers should publicize and act on such reporting mechanisms.
